item.title: Mary Morello, Free Speech Activist Who Defended Explicit Lyrics, Dies at 102
item.description:
Mary Morello, a fiery anti-censorship activist — and the mother of the Rage Against the Machine guitarist Tom Morello — who rose to prominence in the 1980s as a leading opponent of Tipper Gore’s campaign against supposedly salacious artists like Prince and Madonna, died on July 12 at her home in Los Angeles. She was 102.

She died after multiple recent hospitalizations for pneumonia, Mr. Morello said.

A fierce champion for a long list of left-wing causes over the years, Ms. Morello was “the most radical member of the Morello family,” Mr. Morello said in an interview. That was no small feat given his reputation as an outspoken member of a band known for its power-chord polemics against racism, police brutality and corporate greed, including lyrics like “I warm my hands upon the flames of the flag.”

Ms. Morello was an Illinois schoolteacher in her mid-60s when, with a nudge from her son, she retired to found Parents for Rock and Rap in 1987.

Her chief target was the Parents Music Resource Center, or P.M.R.C, started two years earlier by Mrs. Gore, the wife of Senator Al Gore of Tennessee, along with other prominent Washington women, to keep music that had what the group deemed offensive lyrics out of the hands of children.

Mrs. Gore, who served as second lady after her husband became vice president in 1993, became a national lightning rod after a much-publicized Senate hearing in 1985. She and her associates squared off against Frank Zappa and other champions of the outré over what the P.M.R.C. labeled “porn rock.”

Exhibit A was a collection of songs the group labeled the Filthy Fifteen. They included Prince’s lubricious “Darling Nikki” and “Into the Coven” by the Danish heavy metal band Mercyful Fate as well as MTV-friendly (if steamy) tunes like Madonna’s “Dress You Up” and Cyndi Lauper’s “She Bop,” an ode to female masturbation.

The P.M.R.C. lobbied for parental guidance stickers for such material and for record stores to hide prurient albums out of view. It also suggested a Hollywood-style rating system: X for explicit sex; D/A for drug or alcohol references; V for violence; and O for occult- or satanic-themed songs.

Ms. Morello — described by the Chicago Tribune columnist Eric Zorn as a “sweet old lady living in a small white house on a shady suburban street,” never mind her soft spot for Ice-T and Led Zeppelin — was outraged.

“She just couldn’t believe it that there were these stuffy Washington wives who were denying artistic freedom to musicians,” Mr. Morello said. “When I was growing up, there was a lot of Kiss and Alice Cooper being played in the house, and she realized that it was not corrupting my soul.”

Armed with more passion than cash — she started her grass roots organization with $100 — Ms. Morello organized letter-writing campaigns from supporters around the country, and pleaded her First Amendment case on CNN, “The Oprah Winfrey Show” and any other news outlet that would have her.

Her list of the “enemies of freedom” included not just the P.M.R.C., but also allied groups, including the National PTA and the American Medical Association.

“When censorship starts in a democracy,” Ms. Morello wrote in a letter published in The Tribune in 1990, “where does it stop?”

The debate erupted once again in 1989 with the release of the aptly titled “As Nasty as They Wanna Be,” a sex-filled scorcher from the Miami rap group 2 Live Crew that became the first record in American history to be declared legally obscene by a federal court, although the ruling was reversed on appeal in 1992.

“Racial and sexual epithets,” Mrs. Gore wrote in a 1990 editorial in The Washington Post addressing the broader topic, “whether screamed across a street or camouflaged by the rhythms of a song, turn people into objects less than human — easier to degrade, easier to violate, easier to destroy.”

Ms. Morello mounted a full-throated defense of the album. “Nobody speaks that way around me,” she told USA Today in 1990, “but I think it’s a person’s prerogative to speak the way they want. There must be lots of comics in nightclubs who speak similarly and they don’t get harassed.”

Mary Rose Morello, the eldest of three children, was born on Oct. 1, 1923, in Marseilles, Ill., about 80 miles southwest of Chicago. Her father, John Morello, was a tavern owner and later a bank director. Her mother, Gladys (Fitzgerald) Morello, was a nurse.

Her social advocacy started early. “In the 1930s, she helped feed hobos during the Great Depression and supported the coal miners’ struggle to organize,” Tom Morello said in a eulogy at her funeral. “In the 1940s, she helped raise war bonds to defeat the fascists in World War II.”

She received a bachelor’s degree in social studies from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1945, followed by a master’s degree in history from Loyola University Chicago.

Ms. Morello worked as a teacher in Rock Island, Ill., as well as Japan, Spain and West Germany before going to Kenya in 1961 on a teaching program sponsored by Columbia University. At that point, Kenya was coming out of the Mau Mau rebellion, an often-brutal guerrilla offensive against British rule; the country gained formal independence in 1963.

Although the fighters were branded as terrorists in the Western news media, Ms. Morello was a staunch supporter. “They were revolutionaries, anti-colonialists,” she said in a 2000 interview with The Tribune. “So was George Washington. Would George Washington scare you?”

She eventually began a relationship with Ngethe Njoroge, who was allied with the cause and went on to become Kenya’s ambassador to Britain. The couple never married, Tom Morello said, but after she became pregnant with Tom, Ms. Morello returned to the United States, first moving to Harlem.

She and her son eventually settled in Libertyville, Ill., about 40 miles north of Chicago, where she began teaching history and African studies at Libertyville High School.

In a small, conservative town, she and her biracial son faced discrimination. “Someone put a noose and Klan literature on my bulletin board at school,” she recalled in a 2020 interview with the site Elaine Sir.

During the 1980s, Mr. Morello graduated from Harvard and moved to Los Angeles, playing in the band Lock Up. From his position on rock’s front lines, he helped stoke his mother’s interest in the brewing censorship battle.

She ran Parents for Rock and Rap into the late 1990s, picking up friends like Bono, Joan Baez, Bruce Springsteen and Chuck D from the rap group Public Enemy.

In the end, her fight with Mrs. Gore and the others was something of a draw. The P.M.R.C. failed to institute a rating system, although black-and-white parental advisory stickers warning of explicit content became commonplace.

They also became an inadvertent marketing tool, according to many artists and label executives — a badge of authenticity that also turbocharged sales with the promise of forbidden fruit.

In 1996, Ms. Morello was awarded a Hugh M. Hefner First Amendment Award.

In addition to her son, she is survived by five grandchildren.

To celebrate her 100th birthday in 2023, Ms. Morello passed out food at the Midnight Mission in Los Angeles and showed up in a wheelchair to support striking hotel workers.

At his mother’s funeral, Mr. Morello related a story from his childhood, when his mother insisted they join a boycott of grapes led by the United Farm Workers and Cesar Chavez.

For her son, it was epiphany. “There was a new North Star, guiding my thought and action,” he said, “and it was the same one that guided my mom: We have to help those people because we can.”

item.title: ‘The System Reeks’: For a Half-Century, His Populist Message Has Not Changed
item.description:
This week in New Philadelphia, Ohio, at a coffee shop called the Daily Grind, Sherrod Brown told a crowd of 100 or so people about the last big thing he did as a United States senator.

“How many of you benefit from the Social Security Fairness Act?” he asked, referring to bipartisan legislation he co-wrote to get full retirement pay for millions of public workers.

Some hands went up. “Thank you!” a retired teacher named Becky Bender called out.

“Well, the best way to say thank you is to get all your friends to vote for me,” he replied. “It’s going to be a really important year.”

In this really important year, Mr. Brown is a really important Democrat — one of the most important running for office.

He is trying to pull off a difficult political comeback — a quick return to the Senate, where he served three terms before losing his seat in 2024, amid shifting partisan preferences in his state and a tsunami of spending by the cryptocurrency industry to oust him.

This time, he is hoping the environment will prove more favorable. When he lost two years ago, President Trump was on the ballot and Republican enthusiasm was strong. Now Mr. Trump is broadly unpopular, and Mr. Brown is running against Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to the Senate to fill the seat of JD Vance when he left to become vice president.

Democrats see flipping this Ohio Senate seat as key to their hopes of taking back control of the chamber.

On the roster of the party’s hopefuls, though, Mr. Brown cuts a singular figure. He is somehow simultaneously what Democratic voters say they definitely don’t want — and also what they do.

In focus groups and polls and at the ballot box, the Democratic electorate largely clamors for anti-establishment, anti-Washington, younger non-politicians. Mr. Brown is 73. He was first elected to office in 1974. He has spent most of the past three and a half decades working the halls of Capitol Hill.

And yet, as issues of affordability fuel a left-wing insurgency, Mr. Brown is above all else an economic populist. The message more and more people seem to want to hear is the one he’s been preaching for longer than many of them have been alive.

“What he is, is what I think most people desire,” said Dennis Eckart, a former Ohio congressman and longtime friend. “He’s been the senator for the waitress. He’s been the senator for the laborer.”

Republicans, on the other hand, see Mr. Brown as a has-been and a hanger-on, a loser two years ago who will be a loser this year, too, because he’s too far to the left for a state that has spent the last decade tilting to the right.

“It’s pathetic,” Mr. Husted said in an interview.

“It’s either his system, or he was a failure at changing the system,” said Mr. Husted, who was elected to the State Legislature in 2000 and was the secretary of state and the lieutenant governor before being appointed senator. “He can claim either one, but he was a failure one way or the other.”

At the Daily Grind, Mr. Brown worked the room. In contrast to Joseph R. Biden Jr., the former president, or Mitch McConnell, the fading senator — pre-eminent emblems of their respective parties’ aging leadership — Mr. Brown presents on the hustings as comparatively vigorous and fit. In a town and county that voted for President Trump, he finished his remarks, met with local reporters, sat for a picture with a Vietnam veteran in a wheelchair and chatted with one-time and would-be constituents for the better part of an hour.

“We need new blood,” Tammy Dixon, a retired administrative assistant from the Akron area, said in an interview.

But Mr. Brown, she said, was different.

“Who else,” she said, “could take on this fight?”

To know Sherrod Brown’s politics is to know the names of his dogs.

Franklin is a King Charles spaniel with some husky and poodle added in. Walter is a yorkie-poodle mix.

Franklin is for Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Walter is for Walter Reuther.

“The greatest president,” Mr. Brown said in an interview before a meet-and-greet at a bar in North Canton. “And the greatest labor leader.”

The son of a physician, Mr. Brown, a Yale graduate, was four days shy of 22 years old when he was elected to be a state representative — a “liberal” with “labor support” who was already a civil rights, environmental and antiwar activist and organizer in high school, his hometown newspaper, The Mansfield News Journal, reported at the time. “The system reeks,” he said to a reporter. He was re-elected in 1976, 1978 and 1980.

He was elected Ohio’s secretary of state in 1982 and re-elected in 1986 before losing his spot in 1990.

He was elected to Congress in 1992, and he was re-elected in 1994 when so many Democrats were not. He was re-elected five times after that — partly because of his early and ardent opposition to the North American Free Trade Agreement.

NAFTA, he wrote in his 1999 book, “Congress From the Inside,” contributed to anger and cynicism among labor union members as “they saw their wages stagnate and their communities’ factories close and their president send their jobs to Mexico.”

In his 2004 book, “Myths of Free Trade: Why American Trade Policy Has Failed,” he targeted America’s elite.

“If the leaders of our institutions would take the time to listen to people who work with their hands, they might learn something about the reason for workers’ anxiety, about the hopelessness with which many look to the future,” he wrote.

Mr. Brown had remarkable resiliency even as the country’s taste in leaders toggled ceaselessly. He was elected when Gerald Ford was president. He was elected when Jimmy Carter was president. He was elected when Ronald Reagan was president. The year Bill Clinton was elected president, Mr. Brown was elected to the House — the former a so-called New Democrat, the latter a more stubborn acolyte of the New Deal.

Mr. Brown’s 2018 Senate victory, after Mr. Trump had won Ohio in 2016, was sufficiently unlikely that plenty of Democrats wondered whether Mr. Brown himself should run for president.

His message has not changed.

His assessment of the foundational problem of American politics and public policy of the last half-century is that business has been getting bigger and stronger and labor has been getting smaller and weaker — a relentless and systematic diminishment of Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society of the 1960s built atop Roosevelt’s New Deal of the 1930s.

Is it possible that this is a hinge from one political epoch to another? For Democrats, and for him, is the new way the old way?

Mr. Brown walks his dogs.

“History and politics,” he said in the interview in North Canton, “are cyclical.”

In Steubenville, a former steel town hard on the Ohio River, 45 minutes west of Pittsburgh, Mr. Brown walked into the local union hall of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers to applause.

He stood in front of campaign signs. “Workers before billionaires,” said one. “Taking on the rigged system!” said another.

“Sherrod Brown has always stood with us,” Kevan Brown, a union official — no relation — said in his introduction.

Sherrod Brown took the microphone, spotted a man in the crowd and said hello to him by name. He spotted a woman in the crowd and said hello to her by name.

“Always good to see the camo shirts,” he said, nodding to the retired mine workers in their telltale tops. “I know that you’re here for the same reason I’m doing this,” he said. “Because you fear for your country and you see what’s happening. You see the direction we’re going.”

When Mr. Brown first ran for office in 1974, an ad for his candidacy described him as “a change for the better.”

Now, 52 years later, he is advocating for the same sort of change.

“In this country, you see the system, right?” he said.

“You see what happens when corporations are making more and more money,” he said.

“The executives are paid more and more, the profits are bigger, you’re working harder, you’re more productive — and there’s more money going out the door than coming in,” he said.

“That’s why we fight,” he said. “That’s why I’m in this race.”

There are compelling, up-and-coming Democrats in Ohio — Aftab Pureval, 43, the mayor of Cincinnati; Justin Bibb, 39, the mayor of Cleveland; Dani Isaacsohn, 37, the minority leader of the State House. But when the opportunity to run for the Senate arose this year, none of them jumped in.

“As a young person, I wouldn’t want anyone running other than Sherrod,” Mr. Pureval said in an interview. “Affordability, cost of living — that has been Sherrod’s bread and butter and his focus the entire time he’s been in public service.”

Mr. Eckart recalled the speeches Mr. Brown made on the floor of the Ohio House in the 1970s. “He was reincarnating F.D.R.,” he said. “There’s not a whole lot new.”

For Mr. Brown’s critics, this is precisely the problem. “After 32 years of bending the knee to the radical left in Washington,” Nick Puglia, a spokesman for Senate Republicans’ campaign arm, said in a statement, “Sherrod Brown remains completely out of step with Ohio as he fights to hike taxes to give government benefits to illegals.”

Mr. Brown, though, has raised more money than any Democrat running for the Senate except James Talarico of Texas and Jon Ossoff of Georgia. Independent election analysts’ ratings of the race range from a “Republican lean” to a “tossup.” Polling suggests Mr. Brown could win.

“I don’t talk a lot about my opponent, but I’m going to this year,” he said at the coffee shop in New Philadelphia.

“I want to tell you some of the things he’s said,” he said at the bar in North Canton.

“He’s said things like people who are struggling just don’t know how to navigate the real world. He said that people just have to work harder and they have to work smarter and they should just go out and make more money.”

“And then the worst thing, the thing that to me is the most insulting thing,” he said in Steubenville. “The work ethic in this country is ‘broken.’”

“A lie,” Mr. Husted said in the interview.

“He’s never worked in a factory or done hard labor a day in his life,” Mr. Husted said of Mr. Brown.

In his Cole Haan loafers and L.L. Bean slacks and with his characteristically scratchy voice and unfussy air, Mr. Brown mingled in the union hall, lingering with the workers and retirees.

]]>

item.title: Trump Backed Away From a Wall at Big Bend. But the Bulldozers Are Here.
item.description:
Texans were caught off-guard several months ago when the Trump administration appeared poised to construct a 30-foot wall through Big Bend National Park, a rugged expanse of moon-like desert that is a point of pride for many in the state.

But after bipartisan opposition grew, the wall was removed from the federal government’s border construction map. Many exhaled, believing that the West Texas park, with its towering mountains and cliffs, would be spared.

Then the bulldozers arrived this month.

The sight of these earth-moving machines along the Rio Grande near the Santa Elena Canyon, one of the park’s major attractions, pointed to the most significant evidence of border barrier construction in the park. Contractors ripped through mesquite trees and brush and leveled the ground for more than a mile of what appeared to be a future roadway.

Big Bend is beloved by Texans and many across the country, even those who are not among its more than 500,000 annual visitors. It is a place to feel the immense and inhospitable wilderness of West Texas, where the stars at night actually are big and bright.

The construction sparked a fresh wave of anger and outrage from all sorts of people — environmentalists, former park officials, local sheriffs — who again insisted that such infrastructure was unnecessary in a border region so remote and dangerous that people have rarely tried to cross there, even at the peak of unauthorized migration.

Both John Cornyn, the state’s outgoing Republican senator, and James Talarico, the Democrat running to replace him, expressed concern this month about the start of construction inside the park.

“My constituents believe that the 1,000-foot riverbank cliffs and remote Big Bend terrain offers its own source of deterrence,” Mr. Cornyn said in a letter last week to the Homeland Security secretary, Markwayne Mullin.

Other Republican state leaders, including Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton, who defeated Mr. Cornyn in the Senate primary, have not weighed in directly on the construction.

On Friday, a local nonprofit and an outdoor recreation business represented by State Senator Roland Gutierrez, a Democrat, filed a federal suit to try and halt the project. A day earlier, a bipartisan group of Texas legislators sent Mr. Abbott a letter urging him to ask federal officials to stop the construction.

“It’s gotten to the point where people are picking up the torches and marching in the street right now,” said Tex Toler, a former tourism director for Marfa, Texas, northwest of the park. “This is one of Texas’ and the country’s last wild places.”

After days of confusion among West Texas residents, senior Trump administration officials explained their plans and rationale on Thursday. There would be no wall, but there would be construction.

“C.B.P. is building one new access road, improving existing roads, installing detection technology and placing vehicle barriers in limited, strategic locations,” Rodney Scott, the U.S. Customs and Border Protection commissioner, said in a statement.

The park consists of 118 miles of land on the U.S.-Mexico border, and a patrol road is slated to run along much of it. A few areas would have miles of four- to six-foot-tall vehicle barriers.

The bulldozers and excavators have been engaged this month in “survey and design work,” Mr. Scott said.

Fewer than six migrants a day have been encountered crossing from Mexico in recent months in the entire Big Bend patrol sector, which includes the park and hundreds of miles of border, federal statistics show.

Officials have said that while unauthorized crossings are currently at record lows, they could increase in the future.

The Trump administration has been furiously building new border barriers, and Mr. Scott said the Big Bend construction was necessary to fill in gaps. Southwest Valley Constructors, one company currently at work in the region, was awarded a $1.7 billion contract. The company directed questions to federal officials.

“We will not leave Big Bend as an opening for cartels to exploit by shifting their routes and tactics,” Mr. Scott said in the statement.

Many of those who oppose a wall are also against building a patrol road. They include local sheriffs who have insisted that major border infrastructure projects are not necessary.

“What security problem are we trying to solve?” Sheriff Thaddeus Cleveland of nearby Terrell County, a Republican and a former Border Patrol agent, wrote on social media. “Can the same security objective be accomplished more effectively another way?”

On Wednesday, people gathered for a demonstration against the construction at the Santa Elena Canyon. Many carried signs protesting the construction — “Stop the Steel,” “No Wall” — or held handmade depictions of javelinas and other wildlife that could be affected by the construction along the river. Some feared the road plan would require building bridges and blasting along Mariscal Mountain, a remote peak.

“There will be no coming back,” said Michael Ryan, a former Big Bend park ranger who attended the protest. “They’re taking taxpayer dollars to ruin this national park.”

]]>

item.title: Prosecutors Examined Firm With Tie to Judge in Trump Hush Money Trial
item.description:
The U.S. attorney’s office in Chicago has spent the past year investigating a Democratic fund-raising firm once co-owned by the daughter of the judge in President Trump’s hush-money trial in New York, according to court filings and people familiar with the inquiry.

Last August, the U.S. attorney, Andrew S. Boutros of the Northern District of Illinois, directed Authentic Campaigns Inc. to turn over a broad range of internal communications with clients. They included former Vice President Kamala Harris, former President Joseph R. Biden Jr., Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, and the Democratic National Committee, according to a grand jury subpoena reviewed by The New York Times.

Loren Merchan, the daughter of Juan Merchan, a supreme court judge in Manhattan, was the firm’s vice president until late 2024 and was also on the list. The Merchan family has been a frequent target of Mr. Trump and his allies, who have made unsubstantiated claims that the judge was out to get him and that his daughter profited from accusations aired at the trial.

The trial ended with Mr. Trump’s conviction in 2024, in the midst of his campaign for a second term, on 34 felony counts stemming from his efforts to keep a porn star from publicizing her story of a liaison with him.

The firm’s legal team, which included Preet Bharara, the former top federal prosecutor in Manhattan, sought to limit the request. Prosecutors eventually modified the subpoena, narrowing it to focus on a $468 payment from Ms. Harris’s presidential campaign, and emails between Ms. Merchan and her father, according to people with knowledge of the inquiry who requested anonymity to discuss an ongoing legal matter.

It is not clear where the investigation stands. No follow-up subpoenas have been issued to individuals, including Ms. Merchan or Mr. Nellis, suggesting that prosecutors might not be actively working to charge anyone, those people added.

The inquiry is the latest indication of the extent to which U.S. attorneys offices across the country, once largely removed from political machinations in Washington, have increasingly been drawn into the Mr. Trump’s effort to target his adversaries.

In this case, prosecutors sought the subpoena that came from a criminal referral from Republicans on the House Judiciary Committee. The panel made the referral after Mike Nellis, the founder of Authentic Campaigns, refused to provide the committee with confidential emails it was seeking, including those between Ms. Merchan and her father.

“The Trump administration’s targeting of my company is an outrageous abuse of power,” Mr. Nellis said when asked about the investigation. “It is a ridiculous fishing expedition based on conspiracy theories that are completely divorced from reality.”

He accused the department of seeking to seize the “sensitive political communications of my clients who are among Trump’s most prominent political adversaries.”

A Justice Department spokeswoman declined to comment, as did Judge Merchan and Loren Merchan.

The language in the subpoena is virtually identical to claims made by the House committee that Mr. Trump’s conviction in the hush money trial presided over by Judge Merchan was “potentially politically motivated.” The criminal referral also included the contention that “Manhattan district attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation and prosecution of President Donald J. Trump” might have been improper.

The subpoena did not specify what potential crimes might have been committed in the prosecution of Mr. Trump.

In addition to initially requesting information from the Harris and Biden presidential campaigns, Mr. Boutros sought material from Ms. Merchan, Mr. Bragg and one of his deputies, Matthew Colangelo; Mr. Jeffries, the Democratic leader in the House; Ms. Hochul; Senator Adam Schiff, Democrat of California; Representative Daniel Goldman, Democrat of New York; Representative Lauren Underwood, Democrat of Illinois; and the Democratic Party’s House and Senate fund-raising arms as well as the Democratic National Committee.

The career prosecutors who secured the subpoena, Matthew Skiba and William Hogan, both played roles in an ill-fated case against six protesters accused of assaulting federal agents during the White House-directed immigration crackdown in 2025 known as Midway Blitz.

The U.S. attorney’s office in Chicago had to withdraw the charges in that case after defense lawyers raised concerns about the conduct of Mr. Boutros’s prosecutors before a grand jury. That prompted Mr. Boutros, who worked as a prosecutor in the office he now runs, to announce a review of internal procedures.

Mr. Trump saw his hush money trial in New York, which resulted in him becoming the first former president to be convicted on felony charges, as the culmination of a yearslong effort by Democrats to destroy him. He was fighting those charges at the same time that he was defending himself against two separate federal indictments and in an election interference case in Georgia.

Mr. Trump’s public pretrial attacks prompted Judge Merchan to impose a gag order to prevent him from intimidating jurors, prosecutors, witnesses and court staff. Mr. Trump’s lead defense lawyer, Todd Blanche, now the attorney general, argued to rescind the order but was unsuccessful.

By the time the trial started Judge Merchan himself emerged as a main target of the defense, with the president and his allies claiming that Ms. Merchan’s longtime involvement in Democratic politics was proof that the fix was in.

“Judge Juan Merchan is totally compromised, and should be removed from this TRUMP Non-Case immediately. His Daughter, Loren, is a Rabid Trump Hater, who has admitted to having conversations with her father about me, and yet he gagged me,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in March 2024.

The judge did not recuse himself. An ethics complaint filed by Trump allies had no effect on the trial. Mr. Trump’s election to a second term led Judge Merchan to discharge the case without any sentence or penalty.

But Republicans, spurred on by Trump-allied influencers like Laura Loomer, have continued to make the case that the judge, his daughter and other operatives were guilty of wrongdoing.

The Republican chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, Jim Jordan of Ohio, subsequently began demanding documents from the firm. He cited a theory floated by Trump supporters: that Mr. Nellis and Ms. Merchan improperly used Mr. Trump’s prosecution in digital fund-raising pitches on behalf of Democrats. (Mr. Trump aggressively used the criminal indictments against him to raise millions during the campaign.)

“Experts have raised substantial concerns with Judge Merchan, your father, refusing to recuse himself from President Trump’s case despite your work on behalf of President Trump’s political adversaries and the financial benefit that your firm, Authentic Campaigns Inc., could receive from the prosecution and conviction,” Mr. Jordan wrote to Ms. Merchan in August 2024, requesting her correspondence with the judge.

Lawyers for the firm repeatedly argued that Ms. Merchan had no influence over her father’s work decisions and no contact with many of the campaigns the firm did business with.

They accused Mr. Jordan of engaging in a politically motivated “inquisition,” and claimed Ms. Merchan and Mr. Nellis had faced so many death threats from Trump supporters that they needed to hire security.

They refused to hand over most of the documents Mr. Jordan wanted most, calling the request “as baseless as it is dangerous” in a September 2024 letter to Mr. Jordan from Marc Elias, a prominent election lawyer who represented Mr. Nellis.
